note: geometry measured on PEMM00 from a live frame of cn.flytalk.tetris.nearme.gamecenter (2026-10-12, re-measured). Cells are classified by the fraction of a cell's pixels above the HSV thresholds (hsv.min_occupancy), not by a centre sample: a piece the game is animating between two rows covers ~40% of each of them.

gestures.note: the game's own on-screen controls: four buttons along the bottom, measured from a PEMM00 screenshot on 2026-10-12 (13%, 33%, 53%, 81% of the width at 84% of the height). The earlier dialect - a horizontal swipe, a vertical hard-drop swipe and a rotate tap inside the playfield - was a guess and never worked on this game. Positions are fractions so another resolution only needs `screen` updated. One tap on a move button moves the piece one column (the operator's reading of the game).

rotate.note: T1 settled 2026-10-13: the rotation is clockwise (operator's ruling), so one tap advances the piece to the next orientation in clockwise order and `policy_jev` counts taps the same way. Nothing on the device measures the direction, which is why it is written down here: every tap count in the rotate phase depends on it.

move_left.note: one tap moves the piece one column; not verified on the device yet

move_right.note: one tap moves the piece one column; not verified on the device yet

drop.note: Enabled on 2026-10-13: the operator cancelled the no-hard-drop rule. Hard drop is a fast descent — about 0.1 s from wherever the piece is to the floor (operator's figure), not an instant lock. Why that matters here, measured: measured 2026-10-13, the fall is about 0.5 s per row (median 1.78-2.05 rows/s) and about 0.27 s per row in fast mode, so a piece reaches the floor in 3.5-6.5 s while our decisions take 1-6 s. Without the drop, the plan had to be executed over the many frames of that 20 s fall and kept arriving late; with it, the whole execution — shift, then descent — takes ~0.1 s once the decision is made, which is the whole margin this game gives us: the decision has to be made before the piece reaches the floor on its own. Cost, also measured: a tap the device misses is not corrected on a later frame, which the one-shift-per-piece rule had already given up. A turn never drops: the piece has to be there to be shifted next frame. Set enabled=false for a game whose pieces do not fall on their own.

stall.note: A round that has stopped is noticed by the playfield holding still, not by reading text: this app is a Unity surface with nothing in the accessibility tree, and the repo's OCR needs a cloud key. The reading rides in the perception state as `stall`; the inner loop ends the session on it and reports what it measured, and the OUTER loop decides what it means (a finished game, a pause, a dialog and a frozen app all look the same from here) and starts the next round. Similarity is computed on a brightness-normalised, 4x downsampled crop of the playfield, so a screen-wide dimming (measured on the device: 0.61x) is not a change.

measured.source: captures/20261012T061819Z-passive: 43 frames over 30.0 s of the game BEING PLAYED (the board filled from 4 to 15 cells), committed as skills/tetris/samples/session-play (420x855 crops with their real capture times in manifest.json)
measured.note: the first proposal was 'similarity > 95% over 5 s'. Measured on that session: it fires in 22 of its 35 five-second windows while the game is still being played, because a tetromino is ~6000 of the playfield's 359100 pixels and moving it one row changes ~2% of the frame. 0.995 is the middle of the measured gap (0.9823 played, 0.9991 for the panel, whose two captures differ by a 0.61x dimming), not a round number. tests/unit/reflex/test_stall.py re-derives all of these from the committed corpus.

panel.note: The game-over panel, recognised by correlating a committed patch of its title against the same rectangle of each frame. Offline pixels only: this app is a Unity surface, so nothing about it is in the accessibility tree, and the repo's OCR is a cloud service the inner loop must not call. Which glyphs the patch contains (游戏结束) is the operator's reading of the live screen on 2026-10-12 - the code never interprets the text. What is measured is the discrimination: 1.000 on two captures of the panel against 0.051 on six frames of the game being played. roi_ratios is in (x0, y0, x1, y1) like board_roi_ratios, and the patch is resized to that box, so another resolution is a calibration edit.

measured.source: PEMM00 720x1600, 2026-10-12: the operator read 游戏结束 at ~(50%, 37%) and 重新开始 at ~(66%, 64%) off captures/review/panel-grid.png; the patch is that box's crop from samples/panel-gameover.png
measured.note: panel_score is the worst match among samples/panel-{gameover,now}.png and max_playing_score the best among session-000{1,2,21}.png plus reference-{1,2,3}.jpg - a 0.55-wide gap, so the threshold is not a tuned constant. The title's own white text (y[584,612], 28 px tall, centroid x 49.8%) lands on the operator's 50%/37%: an independent check of the box, not of the words.

dimmed_title_band.note: measured on PEMM00: the title box's own mean brightness. The panel *check* cannot use this (a normalised correlation is immune to it), and that is the point: it is what tells 'the panel' from 'the panel behind a dialog'.

restart_flow.note: Starting a new round after the panel takes TWO buttons, which the operator walked through on the device: the panel's own 重新开始 opens a confirm dialog (and dims the screen to 0.61x), and the dialog's left button is what actually starts the round. panel.restart presses them in order and looks at the screen after each, so a first step that already worked is not followed by a second tap into a fresh board. The between-steps check is the panel's own: a normalised correlation still matches the panel behind the dialog, so it cannot be 'the screen got darker' - hence the sequence is calibrated rather than retried. wait_s is how long the app needs before a re-read means anything: 5 s is the operator's figure, not measured.

steps.note: the panel's button. The operator's (66%, 64%) = (475, 1024) is inside the same button; this is its measured centre (the 4-glyph label spans x[447,538] y[1004,1031], the button's body x[408,576] y[980,1050]). Pressing it dims the whole screen to 0.61x and opens the dialog. (the ratios are the measured centre 492/720 and 1015/1600, so the stored point is that pixel exactly)

Measured inside the dialog's un-dimmed body (x[175,343] y[900,960]); the 60x60 px around it is 84% un-dimmed, while the first point in the same frame is 0% un-dimmed. mechanics.note: The game can switch the drop direction mid-session (切换掉落方向) and defines custom shapes (定义方块). gravity_options is the axis set this skill can play and must match simulator.GRAVITIES; shapes is the app's custom shape set as 0/1 bitmaps, empty until a live session records it - the simulator accepts any mask, so nothing needs recompiling when it is filled in. shapes was filled on 2026-10-13 from a live session (captures/play/20261013T064359Z/trace.jsonl), where the falling piece's mask was recorded every frame and normalised to its bounding box: 7 distinct shapes over 15 frames that showed a piece, of 1, 2, 3 and 4 cells — the operator confirmed this game does not always spawn tetrominoes. It is a lower bound, not the whole set. It matters because a 1-cell piece has no orientation to choose from, so 'rotate' is not an action it can take.

fall_speed.note: The operator's ruling, 2026-10-13: the falling speed is NOT constant — the game interleaves a fast mode — so the policy's job is to finish deciding and finish acting as quickly as possible.
fall_speed.measured_from: captures/play/{20261012T143441Z,20261012T141809Z,20261013T064359Z}/trace.jsonl — the piece's own row between consecutive frames, over 55 samples; median 1.78-2.05 rows/s and a fastest of 3.25-3.75 rows/s (about 0.5 s per row, 0.27 s in fast mode)
fall_speed.consequence: a piece crosses ~13 rows in about 6.5 s at the median and about 3.5 s in fast mode. A decision that takes 1-6 s (measured Jev latency, 18 candidates) is therefore comparable to the whole fall, and one that takes 15 s can outlive it. It also explains why a piece shows up in only 1-2 of our frames (0.5-0.6 s each): that is the pace, not lost detections.

jev.mode_note: choice, not noul: noul asks N independent questions ('would r0c3 be the best?') and the policy takes the argmax, which is not a ranking — measured answers spread 0.18-0.54 and do not sum to one, and the winner once landed at position 10 of 18 by the search policy's own ordering. choice asks one question that picks among all candidates and returns a normalised distribution, so the ranking and the margin come out of the same call. The switch is pending the offline comparison in scripts/tetris_jev_modes.py; if it scores worse, revert this line.
jev.option_space_note: placement (default, unchanged) or action. `placement` asks Jev for a rotation and a column and the device needs a turn on one frame and a shift on the next; `action` asks which of the four buttons to press, over a message where the game has already computed what each action would lead to (skills/tetris/policy_actions.py, message v2 in jev_state.build_action_state). The action space is the reference implementation's shape and removes the frame-count constraint, but it needs more calls per piece: it stays opt-in until the offline benchmark (docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-13-jev-decision-redesign.md, T6/T7) has compared them. Addition from 2026-10-13: the operator's ruling that the fall speed varies (fast mode interleaved) and that the policy must decide and act as quickly as possible makes the action space the *wrong* default for this game — it asks one question per action, and at 1-6 s per call that cannot keep up with a piece crossing the board in 3.5-6.5 s. It stays available for experiments; the placement space (one call per piece, executed with a shift and a drop in ~0.1 s) is the shape that fits this pace.
jev.play_message_note: Default set 2026-10-13 from the offline benchmark (T7, docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-13-jev-decision-redesign.md §4): the placement space with the five computed consequence numbers per candidate, asked as one `choice`. On five synthetic states the same arm went from mean regret 25.39 with 0/5 top-1 hits (bare ids) to 0.22 with 4/5 (with consequences) at the cost of 1.8 KB and no measurable latency penalty (2.60 s -> 2.26 s median). The action space measured worse (E 10.63, F 20.13) and needs several calls per piece, which the variable fall speed rules out. Small sample (N=5) and a heuristic judge: the direction is measured, the magnitude is not a verdict.

screen.note: the screenshot size the button fractions below were measured on; the fractions are what matter, this is only what to multiply them by

systemone_timeout_note: Corrected on 2026-10-13. The previous value (15.0) rested on a claim of mine that a piece takes about 20 s to fall and a 7.63 s decision therefore fits — wrong: measured, the fall is about 0.5 s per row (median 1.78-2.05 rows/s) and about 0.27 s per row in fast mode, so a piece crosses the board in 3.5-6.5 s. A timeout longer than the fall is a timeout that loses the piece. 2.5 s is bounded by that budget, and it is safe to be strict because the cost of expiring is small: both policies have an offline plan ready (search for placements, best_plan for actions) and play it immediately rather than waiting.
max_rotate_frames_note: How many frames one piece may spend in the rotate phase before the loop gives up and ends the session with note 'the piece is not turning'. Measured 2026-10-12: eight consecutive frames each asked for two more rotations and the terrain never changed, so 5 s of a 45 s session went into a button that was getting nowhere. An ordinary turn takes one or two frames.
